title: Train Delays in Berlin - Quick Summary
items: **Berlin runs three transport systems and only one of them pays cash.** ICE, IC, RE and RB trains fall under EU rail passenger rights. U-Bahn, tram and bus belong to BVG and pay in free tickets. Check the front of the train before you check the clock.

**The two railway thresholds are 60 and 120 minutes, measured at your destination.** A delay of 60 to 119 minutes pays back **25 percent** of the fare for that single journey, 120 minutes or more pays back **50 percent**. A late departure that catches the time up owes you nothing.

**Nothing under 4 euros is paid out.** That floor is why a delayed S-Bahn or a short regional hop inside Berlin is never worth a claim, and why the rule only starts earning on a real intercity or day-trip ticket.

**At 20 minutes of expected delay your saver ticket stops being locked to that train.** This is the rule that saves the day rather than the money: take the next train that works instead of waiting for yours. At 60 minutes you can also cancel the trip outright and get the full fare back.

**Stranded on the last connection of the day, a taxi or bus is covered up to 120 euros.** It applies when you can no longer reach your destination by 24:00, or on an arrival between 00:00 and 05:00, and only when the railway offers no replacement and cannot be reached. Keep the receipt.

**BVG is a different and much smaller promise.** A U-Bahn, tram or bus more than 20 minutes late through BVG's fault earns a free ticket, and a taxi between 23:00 and 05:00 is reimbursed up to 25 euros. The claim has to be in within **14 days**.
**On a Deutschlandticket you get a flat 1.50 euros per delayed regional journey, capped at 25 percent of the card's value.** Below the payout floor on its own, so bundle several cases into one claim.
**File within three months.** DB is still accepting claims up to twelve months as a transitional practice, but that is goodwill. Ask for the bank transfer instead of the voucher.
